questions.stem: What separates forensic incident response from simply restoring service?

options.text: It investigates what happened, how far it spread, and why, while keeping the evidence intact
options.rationale: Correct: an investigation that preserves evidence integrity.

options.text: It restores service as fast as possible by wiping everything
options.rationale: Wiping destroys the evidence forensics needs.

options.text: It is only a legal formality with no technical work
options.rationale: It is hands-on technical investigation.

options.text: They are the same thing
options.rationale: Restoring service alone doesn't explain what happened.

questions.explanation: Forensic incident response uses forensic techniques during incident response to learn what happened, how far it spread, and why, while preserving evidence. It is investigation with evidence integrity, not only restoring service.
questions.discriminator_tested: Forensic response investigates while preserving evidence integrity.

questions.stem: Malware from an intrusion contains comments in one language and reuses a tool linked to a known hacking group. A manager wants to name that group publicly today. Why should the team be cautious about attack attribution?

options.text: Attribution is uncertain: language strings can be planted and tools are shared or reused, so evidence may be a false flag
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Attribution is certain as soon as a tool matches
options.rationale: Tools are sold, leaked, and reused by other groups.

options.text: Attribution never uses technical evidence
options.rationale: It relies heavily on technical evidence; the issue is how reliable that evidence is.

options.text: Only the attacker's IP address matters for attribution
options.rationale: IP addresses are easily spoofed or borrowed.

questions.explanation: Attack attribution identifies who is behind an attack from evidence such as TTPs, infrastructure, malware, and timing. It identifies the actor, but it is uncertain because evidence can be spoofed or planted.
questions.discriminator_tested: Attribution identifies the actor, but evidence can be spoofed or planted.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the stages of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain?

options.text: Reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Delivery, reconnaissance, weaponization, exploitation, installation, actions on objectives, command and control
options.rationale: Reconnaissance comes first, and C2 comes before actions on objectives.

options.text: Reconnaissance, delivery, weaponization, installation, exploitation, command and control, actions on objectives
options.rationale: Weaponization comes before delivery, and exploitation before installation.

options.text: Weaponization, reconnaissance, exploitation, delivery, command and control, installation, actions on objectives
options.rationale: Several stages are out of order.

questions.explanation: The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain has seven stages: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. It is an ordered, linear model, and stopping any stage disrupts the attack.
questions.discriminator_tested: The Kill Chain is an ordered, linear seven-stage model.

questions.stem: How does the MITRE ATT&CK matrix differ from the Cyber Kill Chain?

options.text: ATT&CK is a non-linear knowledge base of real-world tactics (why) and techniques (how), used to map detection coverage; the Kill Chain is an ordered, linear sequence
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: ATT&CK is a seven-stage linear sequence; the Kill Chain is a matrix
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: They are the same model under different names
options.rationale: Their structure and purpose differ.

options.text: ATT&CK lists only vulnerabilities and their CVSS scores
options.rationale: ATT&CK describes adversary behavior, not vulnerabilities.

questions.explanation: The MITRE ATT&CK matrix is a knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics and techniques. It is not linear: tactics (why) form the columns and techniques (how) sit beneath them, and it is used to map detection coverage.
questions.discriminator_tested: ATT&CK is a non-linear matrix of tactics and techniques; the Kill Chain is linear.

questions.stem: In a Diamond Model analysis of one intrusion event, which feature is the phishing kit with a custom malware loader that the attacker used?

options.text: Capability
options.rationale: Correct: the tools and malware used in the event.

options.text: Adversary
options.rationale: That is the actor behind the event.

options.text: Infrastructure
options.rationale: That covers the servers, domains, and IPs used to deliver and control the attack.

options.text: Victim
options.rationale: That is the target.

questions.explanation: The Diamond Model describes an intrusion event through four connected features: adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim. Analysts pivot between them.
questions.discriminator_tested: Diamond Model: adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim.

questions.stem: Which two of these are TTPs rather than IoCs? (Choose two.)

options.text: The group's habit of phishing finance staff with fake invoices, then using PowerShell to download a loader
options.rationale: Correct: a behavior pattern, covering tactics, techniques, and procedures.

options.text: Using stolen VPN credentials to move between systems at night
options.rationale: Correct: a technique and procedure.

options.text: A specific malicious IP address
options.rationale: That is an IoC.

options.text: A specific malware file hash
options.rationale: That is an IoC.

options.text: A specific domain used for command and control
options.rationale: That is an IoC.

questions.explanation: TTPs are tactics (goals), techniques (methods), and procedures (specific implementations) that describe attacker behavior. They are behavior-based and harder for attackers to change than IoCs such as IPs or hashes.
questions.discriminator_tested: TTPs describe behavior; IoCs are specific observables.

questions.stem: Responders reach a compromised server that is still running. Following the order of volatility for artifacts and sources of evidence, what should they collect first?

options.text: Memory (RAM) and the running state
options.rationale: Correct: it is lost the moment the server is powered off.

options.text: A full disk image
options.rationale: The disk survives a shutdown; memory doesn't.

options.text: Old backup tapes
options.rationale: Those are the least volatile.

options.text: Printed documentation
options.rationale: Not volatile at all.

questions.explanation: Artifacts and sources of evidence include logs, memory, disk images, network captures, registry data, browser history, email, device and cloud data, and metadata. Collect volatile data first: memory and running state before disk.
questions.discriminator_tested: Order of volatility: memory and running state before disk.

questions.stem: How does evidence handling relate to chain of custody?

options.text: Evidence handling is the umbrella: collecting, labeling, storing, transferring, and controlling access to evidence, documented at each step; chain of custody is the documented record within it
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: They are exactly the same
options.rationale: Chain of custody is one part of evidence handling.

options.text: Chain of custody is the broader process, and evidence handling is one log entry within it
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Evidence handling means only putting labels on evidence
options.rationale: Labeling is just one part of it.

questions.explanation: Evidence handling covers collecting, labeling, storing, transferring, and controlling access to evidence, with documentation at every step. It is the umbrella for preservation and chain of custody.
questions.discriminator_tested: Evidence handling is the umbrella for preservation and chain of custody.

questions.stem: An investigator analyzes a seized drive by plugging it straight into a workstation, with no write blocker and no hash taken. What should have been done to preserve the digital evidence?

options.text: Make a bit-for-bit copy through a write blocker, hash the original and the copy, and work only on the copy
options.rationale: Correct: the original stays untouched and its integrity is provable.

options.text: Format the drive first to remove any malware
options.rationale: That destroys the evidence.

options.text: Run antivirus on the original drive
options.rationale: Scanning the original can change it.

options.text: Email a copy of the drive to the team
options.rationale: That neither preserves integrity nor protects the evidence.

questions.explanation: Preserving digital evidence means making bit-for-bit forensic copies, working from the copy, using write blockers, and verifying integrity with hashes. Never examine the original; matching hashes show the copy is unchanged.
questions.discriminator_tested: Never examine the original; matching hashes prove integrity.

questions.stem: A seized laptop goes from the responder to an unnamed courier and then to the lab. The only log entry reads 'received at lab'. What is the problem?

options.text: A gap in the chain of custody: there is no record of who handled the laptop, when, where, or why
options.rationale: Correct: the gap undermines integrity and admissibility.

options.text: The laptop wasn't hashed
options.rationale: Hashing matters, but the problem described is the missing handling record.

options.text: The laptop wasn't patched
options.rationale: Unrelated to evidence handling.

options.text: The laptop runs the wrong operating system
options.rationale: Unrelated.

questions.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented record of who handled evidence, when, where, and why. A gap undermines the integrity and admissibility of the evidence.
questions.discriminator_tested: A chain-of-custody gap undermines integrity and admissibility.
